title: One cloth for two
hookLine: in the forest, birds fly off with Nala's last cloth, and that night he cuts the one they share
carry: partners in dharma share the one cloth

cards: Outside the city, Nala and Damayanti are hungry. Nobody will help them; Pushkara has made sure of that. Then Nala sees birds on the ground with wings that shine like gold, and he thinks: food.
He throws his one cloth over them to catch them. The birds rise into the air, carrying the cloth away. From the sky they speak.
We are the dice, they tell him. We came to take even this. Now a king stands in the forest with nothing on at all.

teach.b: So Damayanti shares hers. The two of them wrap themselves in her single garment and keep walking.
As they go, Nala keeps pointing out the roads. That one goes to Vidarbha, your father's country. Damayanti hears what he isn't saying.
Why are you showing me the roads? I won't leave you. If you want, we'll both go to my father's house, and he'll honor you.
Nala says he won't go back to her family like this. They come to an empty rest house and lie down on the bare ground, and Damayanti, exhausted, falls asleep. Nala can't.
Kali is still inside him. If I go, he thinks, she'll go home to her people. If I stay, she'll suffer with me.
He finds a sword and cuts the cloth in half, gently, so she won't wake. Then he goes. Then he comes back and looks at her.
Then he goes again, torn between love and Kali, until at last he leaves. Now the teaching. Damayanti is what Hindu tradition calls a sahadharmini: a partner in dharma, not only a wife.
At a Hindu wedding the couple take seven steps together by the sacred fire, the saptapadi, and in many tellings of the vows, the seventh step makes them friends.

teach.h: HE GOES, AND COMES BACK, AND GOES.
teach.b: When Nala lost everything, she shared the last thing she had. Even his leaving is love gone wrong, with Kali inside him. The sage keeps telling, because it isn't over.
For today: in Hindu teaching, a marriage, a family, isn't for good times only. Partners in dharma share the one cloth.

how: In the Vana Parva of the Mahabharata, the sage Brihadashva tells Yudhishthira how Nala left Damayanti sleeping in the forest; in this scene the couple are parted.

o: a vow of poverty taken by a king in the forest
cloth, like the one garment Nala and Damayanti share
the golden birds that turn out to be the dice

p: cuts the shared cloth in half

s: they said they were the dice, come to take even his cloth.
at a Hindu wedding the couple walk seven steps together, the saptapadi
in many tellings of the vows the seventh step makes them friends; Damayanti lived it, sharing one cloth.
Nala went back and forth before he left
the story has him leave and return more than once before he finally goes.

games.q: you're Damayanti, walking in the forest with Nala. he keeps pointing out the road to your father's country. what do you do?
o: ask him why he's showing you the roads, and say you won't leave him.
go on alone, ahead of him.
games.why: she refuses to leave and offers to take him to her father's house: a partner in dharma. but that night, while she sleeps, he cuts the cloth and goes.

practice: Bring to mind someone who stayed with you when it would have been easier to go, and see their face; if a time when you left, or were left, comes up too, let it be there without judging it.
Breathe in and remember that they stayed; breathe out and send them a quiet thank you, or, if you pray, hold them in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Vastra, the one cloth they shared, until a husband cuts it in the dark and leaves, and comes back, and leaves.

orig.note: Sanskrit vastra: cloth, garment, like the one Nala and Damayanti share and he cuts in two.

carryVoice: Your line: partners in dharma share the one cloth. Damayanti stayed, with one cloth for two. That's day seven hundred ninety-one.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Nalopakhyana: the birds take Nala's cloth; the shared garment; the roads to Vidarbha; Nala cuts the cloth and leaves Damayanti sleeping)
The Hindu wedding rite: saptapadi, the seven steps (Grihya Sutras; the seventh step's vow of friendship as commonly recited); sahadharmini, the wife as partner in dharma
